title: Krishna Reveals the Vishvarupa
story:
The armies of the Kauravas and the Pandavas stood drawn up on the plain of Kurukshetra, waiting, and in the long pause before the first blow Krishna had been teaching. The despair that had brought Arjuna to his knees at the sight of his own kinsmen drawn up against him was gone. What Krishna had called the supreme mystery — the knowledge of the Self, spoken for his welfare — had dispelled his delusion. But in its place stood a hunger no teaching had yet satisfied. He had heard, at length, of how all beings come into being and pass away again, and of a greatness in Krishna that never diminished. He believed it. Believing was no longer enough. He had been taught the whole of it, and the teaching had left him with one thing still unfulfilled: he wanted to see, with his own eyes, the being who had been speaking to him.

"What you have said of yourself is true," Arjuna said at last. It was not a demand; it was trust. "I desire to behold your sovereign form. If you think that I am able to bear it, show me your eternal Self."

Krishna looked at him with eyes like lotus petals, and did not refuse. "Behold my forms by hundreds and thousands," he said, "divine, of many hues and many shapes. Behold the Adityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the Aswins, the Maruts. Behold innumerable marvels never seen before. Behold, you of the curly hair, the entire universe — everything that moves and everything that does not — gathered together in this body of mine, and whatever else you may wish to see. But you cannot see me with these eyes of yours. I give you celestial sight. Behold my sovereign, mystic nature."

And then he showed him.

The form that rose before Arjuna had many mouths and many eyes, many wondrous aspects, celestial ornaments and weapons uplifted, garlands and robes of heaven, anointed with a fragrance that belonged to no earth. It was full of every wonder, resplendent, without end, its faces turned in every direction at once. Arjuna had known light his whole life — the sun, the fire, the lamps of evening — but nothing he had ever seen came near this. If the light of a thousand suns were to burst forth together in the sky, it would only resemble the light of that Mighty One.

In that single body Arjuna saw the entire universe, divided and subdivided into its many parts, all collected together. His hair stood on end, and he bowed his head and joined his hands, filled with amazement. When he spoke again his voice had changed. "I see all the gods," he said, "and all the varied hosts of creatures, and Brahman seated upon his lotus, and the rishis and the celestial serpents. I see you with arms and stomachs and mouths and eyes beyond counting, on every side, O you of infinite forms. Neither end nor middle nor beginning can I find in you, Lord of the universe, Lord of the universal form."

Still the vision pressed on him, and he looked and looked, unable to turn away. "Bearing your diadem, your mace and your discus," he said, "a mass of energy glowing on every side, I behold you — hard to look upon, blazing like fire at its full height."

There, between two armies that had not yet begun to fight, the man who held the reins of Arjuna's chariot stood revealed as the ground of everything. And the warrior who had asked to see it could only bow before what he had been shown.
reflection: The vision is granted because Arjuna asks for it, and it overwhelms him not with threat but with scale: the whole of creation gathered into one form that has no end, middle, or beginning. What silences him is not fear of the form's power but the sight of every thing he has ever known held, at once, in a single body.
next_story_tease: But the war would not wait long on vision; harder counsel lay ahead on that same field.
hero_scene: Arjuna, head bowed and hands joined, gazes up at Krishna's colossal universal form: countless faces, eyes, arms and weapons radiating light like a thousand suns, with the whole universe gathered inside that one resplendent body on the field of Kurukshetra.
